title: Hello, my name is Ani
goal: Greet anyone safely, say your name, ask someone else's name, and say your first correct Russian sentence — a sentence with no word for "is" at all.
bekal: greet formally and casually, and know the difference
say thank you and excuse me
build "I am X" sentences with no verb

dialogs.title: Диалог — First day of the course
dialogs.intro: Ani, a student from Indonesia, walks into a Russian class in Moscow and sits down next to someone she doesn't know. Notice that not one sentence below uses a word meaning "is" or "am".

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: Hello! My name is Ivan. And you?
lines.literal: be-healthy-you! me (object) — they-call — Ivan. and — you (object)?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. I'm Ani.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: Ani? What a lovely name. Are you a student?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you?

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.

notes: **Russian has no word for "is/am/are" in the present tense.** *Я студентка* is literally just "I student" — two words, nothing linking them. In writing, that missing link is sometimes marked with a dash: *Москва — город* (Moscow is a city). ⚠️ Beginners often hunt for a word for "is" and end up forcing in есть, which is **wrong** here. Есть means "there is", not "is", and you'll learn how to use it in Unit 4.
**Russian has no "a" or "the" either.** There are no articles at all. That is good news that rarely gets mentioned: one of the decisions you make in every English sentence simply disappears.

**Здравствуйте is formal, Привет is casual.** Use Здравствуйте with people you don't know, older people, teachers, officials — anyone you would address as вы. Привет (*pri-VYET*) is only for friends and people your own age. ⚠️ Saying Привет to a lecturer or a passport officer sounds like a child slapping an adult on the back.

**Здравствуйте really is hard to say — and Russians shorten it too.** The first в practically vanishes in fast speech: *ZDRAST-vooy-tye*, or even *ZDRAS-tye* in very casual talk. Don't pronounce it letter by letter.

**Меня зовут literally means "they call me".** Not "my name is". Russians give their name with a sentence whose subject is never named — who "they" are is never explained. Just accept it as one chunk: *Меня зовут ___*. To ask back, **А вас?** ("and you?") is enough; no need to repeat the whole sentence.

**Извините and Простите both mean "sorry", but they don't weigh the same.** Извините (*iz-vi-NEE-tye*) is for small disturbances: interrupting, squeezing past, saying the wrong name. Простите (*pra-STEE-tye*) is for real mistakes — literally "forgive me". Using Простите because you guessed someone's job wrong sounds overdone.

**Пожалуйста: one word, three jobs.** It means "please", "here you go" and "you're welcome" all at once. You will use it dozens of times a day. ⚠️ The spelling is deceptive: written по-жа-луй-ста but pronounced *pa-ZHA-loos-ta* — the й and the middle part melt away.

grammars.title: Sentences without a verb
body: In the present tense, a Russian "X is Y" sentence just puts X and Y side by side. Nothing needs to be added, and adding something is actually wrong.
after: To negate, put **не** (*nye*) right in front of the part you're negating: *Я **не** студент* — I'm not a student. One word, always in front, never changes.

grammars.title: Ты and Вы — two words for "you"
body: Russian separates a familiar "you" from a polite "you", much like French *tu* and *vous* or German *du* and *Sie*. English lost this distinction long ago, but in Russian the choice is **compulsory** and you hear it right away in the verb.

head: ты (ty)
вы (vy)
rows: strangers, older people, bosses, officials — and more than one person

after: ⚠️ A rule of thumb for newcomers: **use вы until a Russian offers ты**. The offer usually sounds like *Давай на ты* ("let's say ty"). Using вы with a peer sounds a little stiff; using ты with a stranger sounds rude. Of the two mistakes, the first is far cheaper.
Вы also means "you" for several people ("you all"), so this one form covers two needs at once.

sections.title: Phrases to keep in your pocket on day one

blocks.text: These ten phrases cover almost all the small talk of day one. Learn them whole, as chunks; the grammar will untangle itself in later units.

head: Русский
Say it
English
rows: Please / Here you go / You're welcome
How do you say this in Russian?

blocks.text: The last two aren't just vocabulary — they're learning tools. Once you can ask "what's this?" and "how do you say it in Russian?", every Russian around you turns into a walking dictionary.

blocks.title: Как дела? and its little trap
items: **Как дела?** (*kak di-LA*) is literally "how are affairs?" — an everyday greeting to people you already know.

⚠️ Unlike English *How are you?*, Как дела? is **not** an empty pleasantry tossed at cashiers or strangers. You ask it of people you know, and the answer is actually listened to. Asking a ticket clerk will just confuse them.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Russian. Remember: there is no word for "is".
Fill in the right ты or вы form (тебя/вас, твои/ваши).
items: To a lecturer in class: Как ____ зовут?
To an official at the airport: Извините, ____ говорите по-английски?
To the neighbors' seven-year-old: Как ____ зовут?
To three friends at once: Как ____ дела?

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Choose the right phrase. Write your answer in Cyrillic.
items: You walk into the lecturers' room at eight in the morning. You say ____.
You didn't catch what someone said. You say ____.
You step on someone's foot on the metro. You say ____.
Someone has just helped you. You say ____.
You take a formal leave from an office. You say ____.

answers: Здравствуйте! — Меня зовут Ани. — Я студентка. — Он не врач. — Как вас зовут? — До свидания!
Меня зовут Ани. — Я не студент. — Очень приятно. — Всё хорошо. — Как вас зовут?
Здравствуйте — Повторите, пожалуйста — Извините — Спасибо — До свидания
